PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 151 — Lesson 175: Hematologic, Infectious & Immune Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate blood-cell production and destruction, hemostasis, thrombosis, infection source and severity, immune competence, medications, and life-stage risk to recognize emergencies, interpret patterns, choose focused testing, begin safe care, and coordinate definitive follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Interpret anemia, leukocyte, and platelet abnormalities by mechanism, severity, trend, and clinical context.
  • Recognize major bleeding, hemolytic crisis, thrombotic microangiopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, neutropenic fever, sepsis, and transfusion reactions.
  • Differentiate primary marrow failure, peripheral destruction or consumption, sequestration, dilution, and reactive laboratory changes.
  • Use pretest probability and validated pathways when evaluating venous thromboembolism rather than ordering isolated tests indiscriminately.
  • Assess infection through source, host, organ dysfunction, epidemiology, antimicrobial exposure, and immune status.
  • Close the loop on abnormal CBC results, cultures, pathology, anticoagulation monitoring, referral, prevention, and return precautions.

Part 1 — The BLOOD-HOST Framework

A laboratory abnormality is not yet a diagnosis. Hemoglobin can fall from blood loss, reduced production, destruction, or dilution. Platelets can fall from laboratory artifact, underproduction, immune destruction, consumption, sequestration, or medication. Fever can represent a self-limited infection, drug reaction, inflammatory disease, malignancy, or life-threatening sepsis.

  • B — Begin with stability: perfusion, oxygenation, mental status, active bleeding, organ dysfunction, and toxic appearance.
  • L — Look at the whole pattern: CBC indices, differential, smear, reticulocytes, coagulation, chemistry, and trends.
  • O — Organize the mechanism: production, loss, destruction, consumption, sequestration, thrombosis, or immune dysregulation.
  • O — Outline the host: age, pregnancy, immune status, cancer, devices, travel, exposures, procedures, and medications.
  • D — Decide dangerous alternatives: shock, sepsis, acute leukemia, TTP, DIC, HIT, PE, major hemorrhage, or transfusion reaction.
  • H — Hunt for the source: focused history, examination, cultures, imaging, and exposure assessment.
  • O — Order discriminating tests: each test should change probability or management.
  • S — Start safe care and select disposition: emergency treatment, targeted therapy, monitoring, prevention, and referral.
  • T — Track to closure: review results, repeat trends when indicated, document response, and give escalation instructions.

Part 2 — First Decision: Is the Patient Physiologically Stable?

Emergency findings include hemodynamic instability, active major bleeding, severe dyspnea or hypoxemia, chest pain with profound anemia, altered mental status, rapidly spreading petechiae or purpura with systemic illness, suspected sepsis, fever during profound neutropenia, severe thrombocytopenia with neurologic or mucosal bleeding, acute hemolysis with kidney injury, or symptoms of pulmonary embolism.

Do not let a “not very abnormal” laboratory value override a critically ill patient, and do not ignore a critical laboratory value because the patient looks comfortable. Recheck unexpected results and specimen quality while responding to the clinical risk.

Part 3 — Read the CBC as a System

Start with hemoglobin and hematocrit, MCV, RBC distribution width, white-cell count and differential, and platelet count. Compare with prior values. Determine whether one lineage or multiple lineages are affected. Pancytopenia suggests a marrow, infiltrative, nutritional, toxic, infectious, hypersplenic, or systemic process more than an isolated peripheral problem.

The peripheral smear can reveal morphology, blasts, schistocytes, spherocytes, target cells, platelet clumping, or abnormal leukocytes. Automated counts are powerful screening data, but morphology and clinical context often reveal the mechanism.

Part 4 — Anemia Is a Mechanism

Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity. Symptoms depend on severity, speed of onset, age, cardiopulmonary reserve, and cause. An abrupt decline can be dangerous even when the absolute hemoglobin is not extremely low; chronic adaptation can make severe anemia appear deceptively tolerated.

Ask about bleeding, stool and menstrual patterns, diet, pregnancy, surgery, chronic kidney or inflammatory disease, medications, alcohol, family history, ethnicity or ancestry relevant to inherited conditions, and constitutional symptoms.

Part 5 — Use MCV, Then Reticulocytes

  • Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassemia, selected chronic inflammatory states, sideroblastic disease, or lead exposure.
  • Normocytic: acute blood loss, kidney disease, inflammation, hemolysis, early deficiency, or marrow disease.
  • Macrocytic: vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, medications, reticulocytosis, or marrow disorders.

The reticulocyte response asks whether the marrow is responding. An appropriately increased response supports blood loss or hemolysis; an inadequate response points toward reduced production, deficient substrate, marrow dysfunction, kidney disease, or suppression.

Part 6 — Iron Deficiency: Replace and Explain

Iron deficiency can cause microcytosis, high RDW, low ferritin, low transferrin saturation, fatigue, pica, restless legs, and reduced exercise tolerance. Ferritin rises with inflammation, so an apparently normal value may not exclude deficiency in an inflammatory context.

The diagnostic task is to identify why iron was lost or not absorbed. Menstrual loss, pregnancy, diet, GI bleeding, celiac disease, bariatric surgery, and other malabsorption matter. Adult iron deficiency—especially with GI symptoms, postmenopausal status, or no clear source—requires cause-directed evaluation rather than indefinite supplementation alone.

Part 7 — Vitamin B12 and Folate

Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause macrocytosis, glossitis, neuropathy, gait change, cognitive symptoms, and impaired proprioception. Neurologic injury can occur without dramatic anemia. Causes include autoimmune gastritis, gastric or ileal surgery, malabsorption, dietary deficiency, and selected medications.

Folate deficiency can also cause macrocytosis but does not produce the same classic neurologic syndrome. Giving folate alone can improve anemia while allowing B12-related neurologic injury to progress. Evaluate the mechanism and replace appropriately.

Part 8 — Anemia of Inflammation and Kidney Disease

Inflammation increases hepcidin, restricting iron availability and reducing erythropoiesis. CKD adds impaired erythropoietin production and can coexist with true iron deficiency, blood loss, or shortened red-cell survival.

Do not attribute every anemia in a patient with CKD to kidney disease. Review trend, iron status, reticulocytes, bleeding, nutrition, medications, and other cell lines. Erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy requires individualized risk-benefit assessment and monitoring.

Part 9 — Hemolysis

Hemolysis may produce anemia, jaundice, dark urine, elevated LDH, reduced haptoglobin, increased indirect bilirubin, and reticulocytosis. The smear and direct antiglobulin test can help distinguish immune from nonimmune mechanisms.

Schistocytes suggest mechanical fragmentation or microangiopathy; spherocytes can occur with immune hemolysis or hereditary membrane disease. Acute hemolysis with chest pain, dyspnea, severe weakness, kidney injury, or hemodynamic compromise requires urgent evaluation.

Part 10 — Sickle Cell Disease: Acute Threats

Sickle cell disease can cause vaso-occlusive pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic dysfunction, infection, priapism, and chronic organ injury. Fever requires urgent evaluation because functional asplenia increases invasive infection risk.

New pulmonary symptoms, hypoxemia, fever, or infiltrate raise concern for acute chest syndrome. Focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise. Pain treatment should be prompt and respectful while simultaneously evaluating the trigger and complication risk.

Part 11 — Leukocytosis: Reactive or Clonal?

Leukocytosis can result from infection, inflammation, corticosteroids, smoking, stress, pregnancy, tissue injury, or hematologic malignancy. Interpret the differential and smear: neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, monocytosis, immature forms, or blasts point toward different pathways.

Persistent unexplained leukocytosis, blasts, basophilia, splenomegaly, cytopenias, or constitutional symptoms requires hematologic evaluation. A single stress-related elevation should be interpreted in the clinical timeline rather than labeled leukemia.

Part 12 — Neutropenia and Febrile Neutropenia

Risk depends on the absolute neutrophil count, depth and anticipated duration of neutropenia, mucosal integrity, comorbidity, and clinical stability. Causes include medications, chemotherapy, viral illness, autoimmune disease, nutritional deficiency, marrow disease, and benign inherited patterns.

Fever with severe neutropenia is an emergency even when the examination is subtle. Inflammatory signs may be muted. Obtain appropriate cultures and begin empiric antimicrobial management promptly according to local protocols without delaying for an obvious source.

Part 13 — Eosinophilia

Eosinophilia may reflect allergy or asthma, drug reaction, parasitic infection, eosinophilic organ disease, adrenal insufficiency, or hematologic malignancy. Travel and exposure history, medications and supplements, rash, pulmonary symptoms, GI symptoms, and organ injury guide the evaluation.

Marked eosinophilia with cardiac, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, or hepatic involvement requires urgent specialty evaluation. Do not prescribe corticosteroids reflexively before considering certain parasitic risks when epidemiology is relevant.

Part 14 — Thrombocytopenia: Confirm It First

An unexpectedly low platelet count may reflect EDTA-related platelet clumping. Review the smear and repeat the count in an appropriate specimen when pseudothrombocytopenia is possible. Then determine whether thrombocytopenia is isolated or part of pancytopenia, hemolysis, liver disease, infection, or coagulation abnormalities.

Bleeding risk depends on count, trajectory, platelet function, medications, trauma, and cause. Mucosal bleeding, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy complications, or rapidly falling platelets increase urgency.

Part 15 — Immune Thrombocytopenia

ITP is usually an isolated thrombocytopenia caused by immune-mediated platelet destruction and impaired production after other causes are considered. The examination may show petechiae, purpura, or mucosal bleeding; splenomegaly or other cytopenias should prompt reconsideration.

Current ASH guidance emphasizes individualized treatment based on bleeding, platelet count, comorbidity, medications, lifestyle, and patient preferences—not the platelet number alone. Major bleeding requires emergency hematology-directed care.

Part 16 — Thrombotic Microangiopathy

Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, schistocytes, neurologic change, kidney injury, fever, or other organ dysfunction raises concern for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or another thrombotic microangiopathy.

Suspected TTP is a hematologic emergency. Do not wait for every confirmatory result before urgent hematology involvement and treatment planning; delay can be fatal.

Part 17 — Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia

HIT is an immune prothrombotic reaction to heparin. Think about timing, magnitude of platelet fall, new thrombosis, skin necrosis, and alternative causes. It is not primarily a bleeding disorder.

Use a validated pretest tool before ordering HIT testing. When clinical probability is meaningful, stop all heparin sources and coordinate non-heparin anticoagulation and testing. An isolated low-probability positive laboratory screen can cause harmful mislabeling.

Part 18 — Coagulation Testing

PT/INR primarily evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways and is used for warfarin monitoring; aPTT evaluates the intrinsic and common pathways and selected unfractionated heparin contexts. Direct oral anticoagulant effect is not reliably quantified by routine PT or aPTT.

Abnormal results may reflect anticoagulants, liver dysfunction, vitamin K deficiency, inhibitors, factor deficiency, consumption, or specimen problems. Interpret the test with bleeding or thrombosis history and medication timing.

Part 19 — Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation

DIC is systemic coagulation activation with consumption of platelets and factors, microvascular thrombosis, bleeding, and organ injury. It can complicate sepsis, obstetric emergencies, trauma, malignancy, and other severe illness.

Patterns can include falling platelets, prolonged coagulation tests, elevated fibrin degradation markers, reduced fibrinogen, and schistocytes, but no single test defines the syndrome. Treat the underlying cause urgently and provide hospital-based supportive management.

Part 20 — Bleeding Pattern Localizes the Defect

Platelet-type bleeding often involves petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, or heavy menstrual bleeding. Coagulation-factor disorders more often produce deep soft-tissue bleeding, hemarthrosis, or delayed procedural bleeding. Mixed disorders and anticoagulants blur this distinction.

Ask about childhood bleeding, dental or surgical hemorrhage, postpartum bleeding, family history, medications, supplements, liver and kidney disease, and alcohol. A normal platelet count does not guarantee normal platelet function.

Part 21 — Venous Thromboembolism

DVT may cause unilateral swelling, pain, warmth, or venous distention; PE may cause dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, or shock. Neither presentation is reliably excluded by a benign-looking examination.

Use clinical pretest probability to choose D-dimer or imaging. A negative D-dimer is most useful in an appropriately selected low-risk patient; a positive result is nonspecific and usually requires definitive evaluation. Hemodynamic instability or high-risk PE features require emergency care.

Part 22 — Anticoagulation Is a System, Not a Prescription

Drug choice and duration depend on indication, kidney and liver function, pregnancy, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, bleeding history, interactions, adherence, cost, and whether the event was provoked. Confirm dose, schedule, missed-dose plan, and peri-procedural ownership.

Monitor for occult bleeding, anemia, renal change, falls, interacting NSAIDs or antiplatelets, and treatment failure. Do not stop anticoagulation abruptly without understanding the thrombotic indication and current risk.

Part 23 — Fever: Source, Host, and Severity

Temperature is one data point. Localize through history and examination while assessing organ dysfunction and host risk. Respiratory, urinary, skin, abdominal, CNS, joint, dental, catheter, surgical, and travel-associated sources require different testing.

Older adults, infants, immunocompromised patients, and those taking antipyretics or corticosteroids may have serious infection without high fever. Conversely, fever alone does not prove bacterial infection or mandate antibiotics.

Part 24 — Sepsis Is Infection With Dangerous Organ Dysfunction

Sepsis is a medical emergency. Suspect it when infection is accompanied by hypotension, altered mental status, respiratory compromise, oliguria, mottling, elevated lactate in context, or other organ dysfunction. Tachycardia and fever are neither required nor specific.

Immediately escalate care, obtain appropriate cultures without delaying therapy, start timely empiric antimicrobials and resuscitation according to protocol, seek source control, and reassess frequently. Narrow or stop therapy when microbiology and clinical evolution support a safer targeted plan.

Part 25 — Culture Stewardship

Cultures are most valuable when a true infection is plausible, the specimen represents the site, and results will change treatment. Collect before antibiotics when feasible and safe, but do not delay urgent therapy in shock. Poor collection creates contamination, unnecessary antibiotics, and diagnostic confusion.

A positive culture must be interpreted as pathogen, colonizer, or contaminant using organism, number of positive sets, source, device, host, and syndrome. A negative culture does not exclude infection after antibiotics or with difficult-to-culture pathogens.

Part 26 — Antimicrobial Stewardship

Before prescribing, define the likely syndrome, severity, expected pathogens, host factors, allergy validity, kidney and liver function, local resistance, and whether drainage or source control is more important than broader medication.

Specify drug, dose, route, duration, monitoring, and stop or reassessment point. Avoid treating asymptomatic colonization except in recognized indications. Reassess nonresponse for wrong diagnosis, resistant pathogen, inadequate adherence, poor penetration, abscess, obstruction, device infection, or immune compromise.

Part 27 — Recurrent or Unusual Infection

Frequent infections do not automatically equal primary immunodeficiency. Consider exposure frequency, anatomic obstruction, asthma, diabetes, HIV, medications, malignancy, malnutrition, loss of splenic function, and secondary immune suppression.

Deep, severe, opportunistic, unusually persistent, or recurrent infections with the same organism or site deserve structured evaluation. Document actual microbiology and response rather than relying only on the number of antibiotic courses.

Part 28 — HIV and Immune Status

Offer HIV testing according to preventive and risk-based recommendations using consent and confidentiality standards. Acute HIV can resemble a nonspecific viral illness; chronic infection may be asymptomatic. A reactive screening test requires the recommended confirmatory algorithm.

For a person with HIV, review viral suppression, CD4 context when relevant, antiretroviral adherence and interactions, immunizations, opportunistic-infection prevention, sexual health, pregnancy plans, and stigma-free continuity. Fever or neurologic symptoms in advanced immunosuppression require a broader urgent differential.

Part 29 — Lymphadenopathy

Characterize localized vs generalized nodes, duration, tenderness, mobility, size, location, associated infection, medications, exposures, and constitutional symptoms. Supraclavicular location, hard or fixed nodes, progressive enlargement, generalized adenopathy, splenomegaly, unexplained fever, drenching sweats, or weight loss raises concern.

Testing should follow the clinical pattern. Persistent concerning adenopathy may require imaging and tissue diagnosis; repeated empiric antibiotics can delay diagnosis of lymphoma, metastatic disease, or nonbacterial illness.

Part 30 — Leukemia and Lymphoma Warning Patterns

Acute leukemia may present with fatigue, infection, fever, bruising, bleeding, bone pain, cytopenias, leukocytosis or even a normal total white count with abnormal cells. Lymphoma may present with painless adenopathy, organ enlargement, pruritus, or constitutional symptoms.

Blasts, pancytopenia, tumor lysis features, coagulopathy, or rapidly progressive symptoms require urgent hematology evaluation. Do not reassure solely because the total WBC is not elevated.

Part 31 — Monoclonal Proteins and Myeloma Clues

Consider plasma-cell disease with unexplained anemia, kidney dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone pain or lytic lesions, recurrent infection, elevated total protein, or neuropathy. A routine serum protein value does not establish the diagnosis.

Use an appropriate monoclonal-protein evaluation and assess organ injury. New severe back pain with neurologic deficits can represent vertebral collapse or cord compression and requires emergency imaging.

Part 32 — Transfusion Reactions

Fever, chills, dyspnea, hypoxemia, hypotension, back pain, chest pain, hemoglobinuria, urticaria, or angioedema during or soon after transfusion can represent a reaction. The first action is to stop the transfusion, maintain access with appropriate fluid per protocol, assess stability, verify identity, and notify the transfusion service.

Do not restart a unit simply because symptoms improve. Acute hemolytic reaction, anaphylaxis, transfusion-associated circulatory overload, transfusion-related acute lung injury, bacterial contamination, and febrile reactions require different management.

Part 33 — Life-Stage Modifiers

Children: age-specific normal ranges, rapid dehydration, occult serious infection, inherited blood disease, and safeguarding alter assessment. Pregnancy/postpartum: physiologic dilution, iron requirements, thrombosis risk, HELLP-spectrum disease, hemorrhage, and medication safety matter. Older adults: marrow disorders, malignancy, anticoagulation, CKD, nutrition, atypical infection, and functional reserve alter thresholds.

Race-based shortcuts are unsafe. Use ancestry only when relevant to inherited risk while evaluating the full patient and avoiding assumptions that delay diagnosis.

Part 34 — Board-Style Case 1: Iron Deficiency

A 68-year-old man has fatigue, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, low MCV, low ferritin, and no visible bleeding.

Reasoning: This supports iron-deficiency anemia, but replacement alone is incomplete. Evaluate occult blood loss and GI causes with appropriate urgency while treating deficiency and assessing cardiopulmonary symptoms.

Part 35 — Board-Style Case 2: TTP Pattern

A 42-year-old has confusion, petechiae, hemoglobin decline, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, kidney injury, and schistocytes.

Reasoning: Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and organ dysfunction suggests TTP or another thrombotic microangiopathy. This requires emergency hematology involvement; do not wait for a routine clinic follow-up.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 3: Febrile Neutropenia

A patient receiving chemotherapy has temperature 38.3°C, chills, ANC 300/µL, and no obvious source.

Reasoning: Profound neutropenia can mute local findings. This is an emergency requiring prompt cultures, empiric antimicrobial management, and risk-based hospital care—not watchful waiting for a source to appear.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 4: Pulmonary Embolism

A postpartum patient develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, oxygen saturation 88%, and presyncope.

Reasoning: The postpartum state increases VTE risk, and hypoxemia plus presyncope suggests potentially high-risk PE. Arrange emergency evaluation; an outpatient D-dimer alone is not a safe endpoint.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 5: Sepsis

An older adult with dysuria becomes confused and tachypneic, BP 82/48 mm Hg, with cool mottled extremities. Temperature is 37.7°C.

Reasoning: Lack of high fever does not exclude sepsis. Suspected infection with shock and organ dysfunction requires immediate emergency treatment, cultures when feasible, timely antimicrobials, resuscitation, source assessment, and repeated reassessment.

Part 39 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Treat anemia without finding the mechanism. Correction: classify production, loss, destruction, and mixed causes.
  • Trap: Low platelets always mean ITP. Correction: confirm the count and assess drugs, liver disease, infection, TMA, DIC, HIT, marrow disease, and other cell lines.
  • Trap: A positive D-dimer diagnoses VTE. Correction: it is nonspecific and must be used within a pretest-probability pathway.
  • Trap: No fever means no serious infection. Correction: immune suppression and older age can mute fever; organ dysfunction determines danger.
  • Trap: Antibiotics alone cure every infection. Correction: abscess, obstruction, infected device, or necrotic tissue may require source control.
  • Trap: A normal total WBC excludes leukemia. Correction: morphology, blasts, cytopenias, symptoms, and trend matter.

Part 40 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Stabilize: identify shock, hypoxemia, major bleeding, severe anemia symptoms, sepsis, or thromboembolic instability.
  2. Read the pattern: trend CBC indices, differential, smear, reticulocytes, coagulation, chemistry, and organ function.
  3. Explain the mechanism: production, loss, destruction, consumption, sequestration, thrombosis, or immune dysfunction.
  4. Define host and source: immune status, exposures, procedures, devices, medications, travel, pregnancy, and comorbidity.
  5. Order selectively: use cultures, imaging, marrow or tissue evaluation, and clot testing only within a coherent pathway.
  6. Treat and control source: address physiology, targeted antimicrobial or hematologic treatment, drainage, anticoagulation, or reversal as appropriate.
  7. Close the loop: own critical results, repeat trends, arrange specialty care, and document return precautions.

High-Yield Summary

  • MCV begins anemia classification; reticulocytes reveal marrow response.
  • Iron deficiency requires replacement and explanation of blood loss or impaired absorption.
  • Confirm unexpected thrombocytopenia and look for TTP, DIC, HIT, liver disease, drugs, infection, or marrow pathology before assuming ITP.
  • Use VTE pretest probability to determine whether D-dimer or imaging is appropriate.
  • Fever during profound neutropenia and suspected sepsis are emergencies even without a clear source.
  • Culture quality, source control, dose, duration, and reassessment are parts of antimicrobial stewardship.
  • Blasts, pancytopenia, concerning lymphadenopathy, or anemia with kidney injury, hypercalcemia, and bone pain require hematologic evaluation.
  • Every anticoagulant, culture, biopsy, abnormal CBC, and referral needs explicit follow-up ownership.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational. Apply current ASH, CDC, IDSA, oncology, transfusion-service, antimicrobial, and local emergency protocols with patient-specific specialist collaboration.
